# 1. Descriptive epidemiology

## Text

> Between 2022 and 2024, `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_total)` residents of the ATS Milano
> territory died before the age of 75 from causes considered avoidable, a median
> of `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_per_year, 0)` deaths per year, with a median age at death of
> `r fmt_num(desc_numbers$median_age, 0)` years
> (IQR `r fmt_num(desc_numbers$iqr_low, 0)`–`r fmt_num(desc_numbers$iqr_high, 0)`).
> Of these, `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_preventable)` (`r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$pct_preventable)`)
> were at least partially preventable and
> `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_treatable)` (`r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$pct_treatable)`) at least
> partially amenable to treatment; the two categories overlap because
> `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_both)` deaths (`r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$pct_both)`) arose from one of
> the seven causes the classification splits equally between the two lists.
> Men accounted for `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_men)` (`r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$pct_men)`) of
> avoidable deaths and women for `r fmt_n(desc_numbers$n_women)`
> (`r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$pct_women)`).
>
> Most avoidable deaths were related to cancer
> (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$cancer$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$cancer$pct)`), diseases of the
> circulatory system (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$circulatory$n)`,
> `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$circulatory$pct)`), and infectious diseases
> (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$infectious$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$infectious$pct)`).
> The `r nrow(desc_numbers$top_causes)` leading individual causes together account for
> `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$pct_top_causes)` of all avoidable deaths:
> `r top_causes_sentence(desc_numbers$top_causes)`.
> Environment and safety (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$environment$n)`,
> `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$environment$pct)`) comprises occupational respiratory disease
> but not traumatic injuries, and mental health and substance use
> (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$mental_health$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$mental_health$pct)`)
> comprises alcohol- and drug-related conditions but not self-harm, since deaths
> from external causes are not part of the ReNCaM register.
>
> Grouped by the mechanism that could have averted the death, most could have
> been avoided by lifestyle and behavioural factors
> (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$lifestyle$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$lifestyle$pct)`, preventable),
> by better clinical management of complications
> (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$tertiary$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$tertiary$pct)`, treatable), and
> by screening programmes (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$screening$n)`,
> `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$screening$pct)`, treatable). The remaining four mechanisms
> account for a minority of deaths, and their small-area models have
> correspondingly wide intervals; all seven are nonetheless fitted and reported.
> Half counts reflect the weight-splitting described in the methods.

::: {.callout-note}
`n_preventable` + `n_treatable` deliberately exceeds `n_total`. The
`avoidability` table below is the mutually exclusive version and does sum to
100%.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Reading notes for §1

- **External causes are absent, and this is the study's largest structural
  limitation.** Transport accidents, falls, self-harm and assault are a
  substantial share of preventable mortality on the published OECD/Eurostat
  list and are not carried by the ReNCaM register. The consequence is
  operational, not just statistical: the *Environment and Safety* layer reduces
  to occupational respiratory disease
  (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$environment$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$environment$pct)`)
  and the *Mental Health* layer contains no self-harm
  (`r fmt_n(desc_numbers$mental_health$n)`, `r fmt_pct(desc_numbers$mental_health$pct)`).
  Neither can support the UOC mapping the February proposal assigned them.
  This belongs in the Discussion as a named limitation.
- **Table 1's cause-group-by-category structure is deterministic.** Circulatory
  disease is almost entirely "both" because the OECD list splits IHD,
  cerebrovascular, hypertensive and aortic aneurysm 50/50. Nothing was
  discovered there.
- **The sex reversal is substantive and is worth a sentence.** Preventable-only
  skews male (smoking, alcohol, occupational exposure); treatable-only skews
  female, because breast and cervical cancer sit on the treatable side.
- **Verify the count of split causes** quoted in the prose against
  `avoidable_lookup_v3.csv`. It is an interpolated scalar and the published list
  carries eight 50/50 causes, not seven; if one has no deaths in this extract,
  say so rather than letting the number look like a transcription error.
- **COVID-19 in a 2022–24 window is post-vaccine COVID**, and its assignment to
  the preventable list is provisional in the OECD classification. One
  acknowledging sentence.
:::

# 2. Covariate distribution and spatial structure

## Text

> The study area comprises `r study_area_summary$n_areas` areal units —
> `r study_area_summary$n_comuni` municipalities and the
> `r study_area_summary$n_nil` Local Identity Units into which the municipality
> of Milan is disaggregated — covering a mean annual resident population of
> `r fmt_n(study_area_summary$mean_annual_population)`.
>
> Crude mortality rates ranged from `r rng_col(crude_geo, "total", 1)` deaths per 100,000 person-years. Standardised
> mortality ratios ranged from `r rng(covariate_table, "Standardised mortality ratio")`.
> Expected counts averaged `r mean_of(covariate_table, "Expected deaths")`
> deaths per areal unit over the three-year period, with a range of
> `r rng(covariate_table, "Expected deaths")`.
> Moran's I on the crude standardised ratios was
> `r fmt_num(moran_crude$statistic, 3)`
> (`r fmt_p(moran_crude$p_value)`, `r fmt_n(moran_crude$n_sim)` permutations),
> which does not on its own establish spatial structure: crude ratios in areas
> with expected counts as low as
> `r fmt_num(min_of(covariate_table, "Expected deaths"), 2)` are dominated by
> Poisson noise, and a global statistic computed on them has little power. The
> case for a spatially structured specification rests instead on the residuals
> of the unadjusted model, where Moran's I is
> `r by_model(moran_residual, "M1", "statistic")`
> (`r by_model(moran_residual, "M1", "p_value", fmt = fmt_p)`) — see §3.
>
> The Italian Deprivation Index ranged from
> `r rng(covariate_table, "Deprivation Index")` in summed z-score units, with a
> median of `r median_of(covariate_table, "Deprivation Index")`, which sits
> below the national average of zero: the ATS Milano territory is among the more
> affluent in the country.
>
> Nitrogen dioxide averaged `r mean_of(covariate_table, "NO2 (ug/m3)")` µg/m³
> (SD `r sd_of(covariate_table, "NO2 (ug/m3)")`), while PM2.5 averaged
> `r mean_of(covariate_table, "PM2.5 (ug/m3)")` µg/m³
> (SD `r sd_of(covariate_table, "PM2.5 (ug/m3)")`), showing markedly less
> contrast across the study area. NO₂ was therefore selected as the primary
> environmental exposure. The two pollutants correlate at
> `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "no2", "pm25"), 2)` (Spearman),
> which is why they are mutually attenuating when entered jointly and are
> instead compared across M5 and M7.
>
> Primary care supply averaged
> `r mean_of(covariate_table, "GP-equivalents per 1,000")` general-practitioner
> equivalents per 1,000 residents
> (SD `r sd_of(covariate_table, "GP-equivalents per 1,000")`), ranging
> `r rng(covariate_table, "GP-equivalents per 1,000")` across areal units —
> equivalently, between roughly
> `r recip_of(covariate_table, "GP-equivalents per 1,000", "max")` and
> `r recip_of(covariate_table, "GP-equivalents per 1,000", "min")`
> residents per full-time-equivalent general practitioner. The measure is a
> supply density rather than a headcount: each general practitioner is shared
> out across their registered list, so an area's value is the sum of
> 1 / list size over its residents. Its rank correlation with the Deprivation
> Index was
> `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "gp_density", "di_score"), 2)`
> (Spearman); the inverse care law predicts a negative value, and the sign here
> should be read off that number rather than assumed. The modelled association,
> conditional on deprivation and spatial structure, is reported in M5.
>
> The testable implication of the DAG — that primary care capacity is
> conditionally independent of the outcome given deprivation and location — was
> assessed by correlating M4's residuals with primary care capacity. The
> correlation was `r fmt_num(cond_independence$estimate, 3)`
> (`r fmt_p(cond_independence$p_value)`), so the implication
> `r ifelse(cond_independence$p_value > 0.05, "was not contradicted", "was contradicted")`.
> Note that surviving one testable implication is weak evidence for a graph;
> failing one would have been strong evidence against it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading notes for §2

- **Every covariate is a partial measurement of one latent thing.** Travel time
  to hub against NO₂ is
  `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "t_hub_mean", "no2"), 3)`;
  t_hub against t_centre
  `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "t_hub_mean", "t_centre_mean"), 3)`;
  IVSM against t_centre
  `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "ivsm", "t_centre_mean"), 3)`.
  That common factor is urban–rural position, and it is why §4.4's NO₂ and
  primary-care coefficients move between M2 and M5, and why §6.3 needs a
  specification ladder rather than a single fit.
- **The deprivation index is right-skewed with one extreme value**
  (max `r max_of(covariate_table, "Deprivation Index")` against a median of
  `r median_of(covariate_table, "Deprivation Index")`). The headline
  coefficient is per SD, so a single area can move it. Report the winsorised
  refit alongside.
- **The change of resolution is the methodological gain, not a technical
  detail.** Within-Milan SD of the deprivation index is
  `r fmt_num(deprivation_resolution$nil_sd_area, 3)` against an overall study
  SD of `r fmt_num(deprivation_resolution$overall_sd, 3)`. Under the previous
  municipality-level construction that within-Milan figure was exactly zero.
- **The primary-care result is a finding, not a nuisance.** A rank correlation
  with deprivation of
  `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "gp_density", "di_score"), 2)`
  means the inverse care law is not operating in this territory.
:::

## Primary care: coverage of the indicator

The indicator and the modelling geography are built from different registers,
so their coverage has to be checked rather than assumed: an area with no
indicator is imputed from its neighbours by `add_covariate()`, which warns but
does not stop.

```{r gp-density-audit}
gp_density_audit |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) fmt_num(x, 2))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Modelled areas", "Indicator rows", "Matched",
                      "Areas without indicator", "Unmapped indicator rows",
                      "Unmapped population", "% population unmapped"),
        caption = "Overlap between the primary-care indicator and the modelling geography.")
```

```{r gp-density-audit-keys, results="asis"}
none_if_empty <- function(x) if (length(x)) paste(x, collapse = ", ") else "none"
cat(sprintf(
  "Modelled areas with no indicator: %s. Indicator rows with no modelled area: %s.\n",
  none_if_empty(attr(gp_density_audit, "area_no_indicator")),
  none_if_empty(attr(gp_density_audit, "indicator_no_area"))
))
```

# 3. Model comparison

## Text

> `r convergence_sentence(model_diagnostics)`
>
> The comparison by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation is shown in
> Table 3. `r loo_sentence(tbl_loo)`
> `r pareto_sentence(pareto_audit, "M5")`
> Moran's I on M5 residuals was `r by_model(moran_residual, "M5", "statistic")`
> (`r by_model(moran_residual, "M5", "p_value", fmt = fmt_p)`), indicating
> the spatial component
> `r moran_verdict(moran_residual, "M5")`
> absorbed the structure present in the crude ratios.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading notes for §3

- **Compare `elpd diff` against `SE diff`, never against `SE`.** The individual
  standard errors are computed on 279 pointwise terms; the difference is
  computed on *paired* pointwise differences and is much smaller. M4 and M5
  each carry an SE near
  `r fmt_num(tbl_loo$se_elpd[tbl_loo$model == "M4"], 1)` while the difference
  between them has an SE of
  `r fmt_num(abs(tbl_loo$se_diff[tbl_loo$model == "M5"]), 1)`.
- **The spatial term does more predictive work than the covariates.**
  M1 → M2 (covariates only) and M1 → M3 (spatial only) are the two increments
  to read off the table; the second is roughly twice the first. M4 → M5, which
  adds NO₂ and primary care, is negative.
- **M4 wins on LOO but M5 is the reported model.** They are indistinguishable
  predictively, and M5 is the specification that answers the substantive
  question — how much of the geography the measured determinants account for.
  Prediction and estimation are not the same criterion, and the choice is made
  on the second.
- **M3 and M4 being indistinguishable does not weaken the deprivation
  coefficient.** The BYM2 field can reproduce a smooth covariate's spatial
  pattern for prediction while the coefficient remains identified by
  within-neighbourhood contrast. See §4.4, where the estimate is stable to
  three decimals across five specifications.
- **The residual Moran's I sequence is the argument for BYM2.** M1 → M2 shows
  that covariates alone do not remove the spatial structure; M2 → M3 shows that
  the spatial term does.
- **Mild over-smoothing across M3–M7** (residual I slightly negative) is within
  noise at this n. M6 is the most affected.
:::

```{r diagnostics-table}
model_diagnostics |>
  mutate(across(c(rhat_max, ebfmi_min, rho), \(x) fmt_num(x, 3)),
         across(c(ess_min, n_divergent, treedepth_hits), \(x) fmt_n(x)),
         pct_divergent = fmt_pct(pct_divergent),
         waic = fmt_num(waic, 1)) |>
  select(model, n_draws, rhat_max, ess_min, n_divergent, pct_divergent,
         treedepth_hits, ebfmi_min, rho, waic) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Draws", "Max R-hat", "Min ESS", "Divergent",
                      "% divergent", "Treedepth hits", "Min E-BFMI", "rho",
                      "WAIC"),
        caption = "Convergence and sampler diagnostics, M1–M7.")
```

```{r loo-table}
tbl_loo |>
  mutate(across(c(elpd_loo, se_elpd, p_loo, looic, elpd_diff, se_diff),
                \(x) fmt_num(x, 1)),
         ratio = fmt_num(ratio, 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "elpd LOO", "SE", "p_loo", "LOOIC",
                      "elpd diff", "SE diff", "|diff|/SE", "Verdict",
                      "Pareto-k > 0.7"),
        caption = "Leave-one-out comparison, ordered best first. Higher elpd is better.")
```

```{r moran-table}
moran_residual |>
  mutate(across(c(statistic, post_mean, post_low, post_high), \(x) fmt_num(x, 3)),
         p_value = fmt_p(p_value)) |>
  select(model, statistic, p_value, post_mean, post_low, post_high) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Moran's I", "p", "Posterior mean I",
                      "2.5%", "97.5%"),
        caption = "Moran's I on Pearson residuals. Computed on residuals, not on smoothed relative risks — the latter are spatially autocorrelated by construction.")
```

```{r pareto-table}
if (nrow(pareto_audit)) {
  pareto_audit |>
    mutate(across(c(pareto_k, expected, population), \(x) fmt_num(x, 2))) |>
    kable(caption = "Areas where the leave-one-out approximation is unreliable under M5, ordered by expected count.")
} else {
  cat("No area exceeded a Pareto-k of 0.7 under M5.\n")
}
```

# 4. Avoidable mortality estimates and risk surface

## 4.1 Residual excess

> Summed across the study area, `r fmt_num(excess$total$excess_per_year, 0)`
> deaths per year occurred beyond what age and sex structure, deprivation, air
> pollution and primary care capacity jointly predict (95% credible interval
> `r fmt_num(excess$total$ci_low, 0)` to `r fmt_num(excess$total$ci_high, 0)`),
> which is `r fmt_pct(excess$total$pct_of_total)` of overall avoidable
> mortality. This sum is a calibration check rather than a result: residual
> excess summed over all areas is centred on zero by construction in a
> well-fitted model, and it is the distribution across areas, not the total,
> that carries information.
>
> Adding the covariates to the unadjusted model reduced between-area
> variance by `r fmt_pct(variance_reduction$reduction$pct_reduction)`
> (95% CrI `r fmt_pct(variance_reduction$reduction$ci_low)` to
> `r fmt_pct(variance_reduction$reduction$ci_high)`).
> `r variance_verdict(variance_reduction)`
>
> `r excess$n_flagged` areas had a posterior probability above
> `r excess$prob_cutoff` that their residual relative risk exceeded
> `r excess$threshold`.

```{r variance-table}
variance_reduction$by_model |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) fmt_num(x, 3))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Residual variance", "2.5%", "97.5%",
                      "Residual SD", "2.5%", "97.5%", "rho"),
        caption = "Between-area residual variation before and after adjustment.")
```

```{r excess-flagged-table}
excess$per_area |>
  filter(flagged) |>
  arrange(desc(excess)) |>
  mutate(across(c(excess, excess_low, excess_high, rr_resid), \(x) fmt_num(x, 2)),
         p_exceed = fmt_num(p_exceed, 2)) |>
  select(area, observed, expected, excess, excess_low, excess_high,
         rr_resid, p_exceed) |>
  # Interpolated, not typed. This header said 1.20 for several runs while the
  # pipeline was flagging on 1.10, because the number was a literal in a string.
  kable(col.names = c("Area", "Observed", "Expected", "Excess/yr", "2.5%",
                      "97.5%", "Residual RR",
                      sprintf("P(RR > %.2f)", excess$threshold)),
        caption = "Areas flagged as showing residual excess under M5.")
```

```{r fig-excess, fig.cap="Residual excess avoidable deaths per year under M5."}

```


## 4.2 Risk surface

> Smoothed relative risks ranged from `r rr_range(aug_M3)` (Figure 4.3), a
> considerably narrower range than the standardised mortality ratios.
> At the `r 0.80` probability cutoff, `r n_exceeding(aug_M3, 0.80)` areas were
> classified as showing excess. The remaining areas are not evidence of evenly
> distributed risk; they reflect the model's expected behaviour given lower
> counts, which produce broader posteriors.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading notes for §4

- **The contrast between §4.1 and §4.2 is the result.**
  `r n_exceeding(aug_M3, 0.80)` areas exceed the cutoff on the unadjusted M3
  surface; `r excess$n_flagged` survive on the M5 residual surface. Deprivation
  accounts for the difference. The geography of avoidable death in this
  territory is largely the geography of deprivation, and only the surviving
  area is doing something the covariates cannot explain.
- **Named clusters must come from the flagged-area table, not from memory.**
  Two cluster names carried over from an earlier run were removed here; any
  geography in the thesis text should be re-derived from the table above and
  the area codes resolved to names.
- **The residual-excess total is a calibration check**, not a finding of "no
  excess mortality". See the wording in §4.1.
- **Deprivation is the single most robust estimate in the study.** It sits at
  `r fmt_num(min(model_coefficients$estimate[model_coefficients$term == "di_score_z"]), 3)`–`r fmt_num(max(model_coefficients$estimate[model_coefficients$term == "di_score_z"]), 3)`
  per SD across every specification in §4.4 — two spatial parameterisations and
  two pollutants — and does not move.
- **NO₂ and primary care are significant in M2 and null everywhere else, and
  both point below 1.** M2 carries no spatial term, so in that fit the two are
  proxying urban position, which in this territory is confounded with
  affluence and service supply. Once BYM2 absorbs position they have nothing
  left to explain. A protective coefficient for nitrogen dioxide should be read
  as a confounding signature, not as an effect.
:::

# 5. Avoidable mortality by mechanism

> The smoothed risk surfaces for all seven strata are shown in Figure 5.1.
> `r mechanism_sentence(mechanism_table)`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading notes for §5

- **Five strata flag no areas, and that is power, not safety.** Screening
  carries `r fmt_n(mechanism_table$deaths[mechanism_table$mechanism == "Screening"])`
  deaths and Gender and Reproductive Health
  `r fmt_n(mechanism_table$deaths[mechanism_table$mechanism == "Gender and Reproductive Health"])`,
  spread across `r nrow(sf::st_drop_geometry(aug_M3))` areas. Empty rows should
  not be read as reassuring findings.
- **rho is not identified in the smaller strata.** The intervals span most of
  the unit interval and overlap across every pair; the spread of point
  estimates is prior, not signal.
- **The two well-powered surfaces are largely the same map.** Lifestyle and
  NCDs against Tertiary prevention rank at
  `r fmt_num(mechanism_concordance$long$rho[1], 3)`. The proposal's premise was that
  each thematic layer hands a different geography to a different UOC; on this
  evidence the two largest layers hand nearly the same geography to two
  different UOCs. The defensible reading is that the same neighbourhoods need
  both primary prevention and better clinical management — an argument for
  coordinated action rather than parallel vertical programmes — but it has to
  be argued rather than passed over.
- **Low concordance among the small strata is not evidence of distinct
  geography.** Where at least one surface is noise, two surfaces are
  uncorrelated by construction.
:::

# 6. Stroke sub-model and negative controls

The reference outcome here is **I63 cerebral infarction, all ages**, not
cerebrovascular mortality 0–74. Two reasons, both settled before any
coefficient was read. The 75-year ceiling belongs to the OECD/Eurostat
avoidability definition rather than to the clinical question — an ischaemic
stroke at 90 is as treatable as one at 60 — and mechanical thrombectomy acts on
cerebral infarction alone, while the haemorrhagic subtypes are a different care
channel. An outcome pooling them dilutes any access effect by construction. The
original 0–74 cerebrovascular proposition is retained below as a comparison,
and in the stroke sub-report in full.

## Text

> `r stroke_time_sentence(stroke_times_table)`
>
> `r stroke_subtype_sentence(stroke_subtypes)`
>
> `r i63_smoothing_sentence(i63_smoothing, i63_exceedance)`
>
> `r control_sentence(control_table)`

::: {.callout-warning}
The negative control **exposure** (T3) has not been fitted: the variable has not
been chosen. The panel below therefore has three of its four slots filled. See
the work log for two candidate exposures.
:::

## 6.3 Does travel time predict risk?

The specification follows from the causal graph rather than from convention.
The graph has a single backdoor path from travel time to mortality — travel
time is set by where hubs were sited, hubs were sited where the population
already was, and that same urban–rural position drives deprivation, air
quality and primary care supply, each of which acts on mortality. That latent
position is unmeasured, so the adjustment set is its three measured children on
the outcome side: **deprivation, NO₂ and primary care density**. Reperfusion
timing and case fatality are how the exposure acts, not confounders of it, and
are deliberately absent — conditioning on either would estimate a controlled
direct effect that is zero by construction.

The four rungs below differ in how much spatial variation they remove from the
exposure before estimating.

| Specification | The question it answers | What a null means here |
|---|---|---|
| **GLM, exposure only** | Across the whole territory, do areas further from a hub die more? | No marginal association. Confounded by everything on the backdoor path. |
| **GLM + adjustment set** *(reference)* | The total effect of access, with the one backdoor path closed through measured proxies. | Either no effect, or residual confounding by the part of the urban–rural gradient the three covariates fail to capture. |
| **BYM2 + adjustment set** | *Within a neighbourhood of similar spatial risk*, does travel time add anything? | Not the same estimand. The random effect is itself an estimate of the latent confounder, and travel time is very nearly a deterministic function of position, so conditioning on a smooth spatial surface conditions on the exposure. What is left is the exposure's non-spatial residual. |
| **ESF + adjustment set** | The same, partitioning spatial variation differently. | Agreement with BYM2 means the absorption is not an artefact of how the spatial term is parameterised. |

The reference model is the second rung. The third and fourth are reported as a
bound, not as a correction to it: they answer a question the thesis did not
ask, and a null there is uninformative about access. The intercept-only BYM2
appears separately in §6.4, where it is descriptive and has no exposure term
to report.

```{r i63-engine-table}
i63_engine_table |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, ci_low, ci_high), \(x) fmt_num(x, 3))) |>
  select(model, label, estimate, ci_low, ci_high, ess, rhat) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Specification", "Term", "RR per SD", "2.5%", "97.5%",
                      "ESS", "R-hat"),
        caption = "The specification ladder. I63, all ages, against travel time to the nearest thrombectomy hub. Row two is the reference model; rows three and four remove the exposure's spatial contrast along with the confounding.")
```

Read the ladder top to bottom. If the estimate collapses toward the null
between rungs two and three, that is the absorption the graph predicts, not
evidence that access does not matter; a low effective sample size concentrated
on the exposure coefficient, while the intercept samples freely, is its
signature. If instead rungs one and two differ substantially, the adjustment
set is doing real work and the confounding was material.

```{r allage-table}
allage_table |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, ci_low, ci_high), \(x) fmt_num(x, 3))) |>
  select(model, label, estimate, ci_low, ci_high, ess, rhat) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Outcome ~ exposure", "Term", "RR per SD", "2.5%",
                      "97.5%", "ESS", "R-hat"),
        caption = "All-age outcomes and destination sets under BYM2. Read alongside the feasibility verdict above: a tight interval on an unmodellable outcome is the prior speaking.")
```

## 6.6 Interpretation

The tracer coefficient is **not** null. Travel time to the nearest thrombectomy
hub carries a relative risk of
`r fmt_ci(control_table$estimate[control_table$role == "Tracer" & control_table$scored], control_table$ci_low[control_table$role == "Tracer" & control_table$scored], control_table$ci_high[control_table$role == "Tracer" & control_table$scored], 3)`
per standard deviation on all-age I63 mortality, the negative control outcome
is null, and the positive control behaves as pre-specified. This section
therefore enumerates what a *positive* coefficient of this size is consistent
with, which is not the same list as the one a null would have required.

**The magnitude is the problem, and §6.2 is where it bites.** One standard
deviation of the exposure is roughly
`r fmt_num(.cov_row(stroke_times_table, "Nearest thrombectomy hub (level II), minutes")[["sd"]], 1)`
minutes. §6.2 establishes, before any model was fitted, that thrombectomy could
touch on the order of 10% of the reference outcome, so even a large reduction
in case fatality within the eligible subset moves total I63 mortality by well
under one per cent. An estimated effect of this magnitude is therefore an order
of magnitude too large to be an access-to-thrombectomy effect. Whatever the
coefficient is measuring, the pre-specified mechanism cannot generate it.

Three explanations remain, in descending order of how well the design
constrains them.

1. **Residual confounding by urban–rural position.** The leading candidate.
   §6.3's adjustment set is three measured children of a latent gradient, not
   the gradient itself, and §2 shows travel time correlating with NO₂ at
   `r fmt_num(cor_between(covariate_correlations, "t_hub_mean", "no2"), 3)`.
   The estimate survives all four rungs of the ladder at a similar magnitude,
   which is consistent with a real association *and* with a confounder the
   covariates only partly capture — the ladder cannot separate those. The
   negative control **exposure** (T3) is the test that would, and it has not
   been fitted; until it is, this explanation cannot be ranked against the
   others.
2. **Differential outcome misclassification.** §6.2 records
   `r fmt_n(stroke_subtypes$deaths[grepl("^I64", stroke_subtypes$subtype)])`
   deaths coded I64, stroke type not specified, against
   `r fmt_n(stroke_subtypes$deaths[grepl("^I63", stroke_subtypes$subtype)])`
   coded I63. Certification specificity varies by certifying hospital, and
   hospital catchment is a function of the same geography as the exposure. If
   peripheral areas code proportionally more I63 while central areas default to
   I64, that alone manufactures a travel-time gradient in I63 mortality with no
   clinical content. This is directly testable by refitting the reference
   specification with I64 as the outcome: an opposing gradient there would
   largely settle it.
3. **A real access effect operating through the whole time-critical care
   chain.** Not thrombectomy alone — the arithmetic above rules that out — but
   dispatch, door-to-needle time, stroke-unit admission and the rest of the
   pathway, for which travel time to a level-II centre is a proxy. This is the
   substantively interesting reading and the least well supported: the design
   was built to interrogate thrombectomy access specifically, and it cannot
   distinguish this from explanation 1.

Two constraints from earlier sections continue to apply and are worth restating
because they bound any of the three readings.

- **Exposure misclassification attenuates.** Routed time from a
  population-weighted origin to the nearest hub is not the time a patient
  actually takes, which includes dispatch, bypass protocols and drip-and-ship
  transfers. That error is non-differential with respect to the outcome, so it
  biases toward the null and the true association under reading 3 would be
  larger still.
- **The spatial rungs answer a different question.** The reference model
  carries no spatial random effect, precisely because that term and the
  exposure describe the same smooth variation. §6.3's BYM2 and ESF rungs are
  reported as a bound, not as a correction; note that the point estimate barely
  moves across them while precision falls, and that the effective sample size
  collapse is specific to BYM2 and absent under ESF.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading notes for §6

- **The outcome change must stay visible.** The original 0–74 cerebrovascular
  specification returns a null and the revised one does not. The reasoning for
  the change was settled before any coefficient was read and both are reported;
  keep it that way in the Methods, because a reader who discovers the switch
  later will discount everything after it.
- **§6.2's arithmetic is the strongest paragraph in the chapter** and it argues
  against the headline result. Present it that way rather than as a
  feasibility footnote.
- **Fit T3.** A negative control exposure that tracks urban–rural position with
  no path to cerebral infarction — travel time to the nearest post office,
  library or municipal registry office would serve — is a single additional fit
  on machinery that already exists, and it is the direct test of whether the
  tracer measures access or area character. Either result is reportable.
- **Fit I64 as an outcome** for the misclassification test described above.
- **The control panel passes.** The verdict column previously scored adjustment
  covariates against each arm's expectation and produced four spurious
  failures; the designated exposure in each arm is now the only row scored.
:::
